title: Die drei Faulen
source: Brüder Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen, Band 2, 7. Auflage (Ausgabe letzter Hand), Dieterich, Göttingen 1857, KHM 151. Text from Wikisource (twice proofread against the original). Fresh translation made directly from the German; 1857 spelling preserved (daß, wußte, ließ).
about: KHM 151 is a joke dressed as a fairy tale: a dying king promises his throne to whichever of his three sons is laziest, and each son boasts an ever more absurd feat of idleness — not shutting his eyes against a falling drop, not pulling his feet back from the fire, not lifting a hand to save his own neck from the noose. The third and most outrageous claim wins outright; there is no moral beyond the joke itself.

sentences.t: Ein König hatte drei Söhne, die waren ihm alle gleich lieb,
sentences.l: A king had three sons, they were to him all equally dear,
sentences.i: A king had three sons, and he held them all equally dear,
sentences.n: “die waren ihm alle gleich lieb” uses jemandem lieb sein, to be dear to someone, with the dative “ihm”; German reaches for this rather than a verb of loving. “gleich” here is ‘equally,’ not ‘at once.’

sentences.t: und er wußte nicht welchen er zum König nach seinem Tode bestimmen sollte.
sentences.l: and he did not know which one he should appoint as king after his death.
sentences.i: and he did not know which of them to name king after his death.
sentences.n: “zum König bestimmen” = to designate as king; zu plus the dative marks the office someone is appointed to. “wußte” is the 1857 spelling of wusste.

sentences.t: Als die Zeit kam, daß er sterben wollte, rief er sie vor sein Bett und sprach „liebe Kinder, ich habe etwas bei mir bedacht, das will ich euch eröffnen:
sentences.l: When the time came that he wanted to die, he called them before his bed and said “dear children, I have considered something within myself, that I will disclose to you:
sentences.i: When the time came for him to die, he called them to his bedside and said, “Dear children, I have turned something over in my own mind, and I will tell you what it is:
sentences.n: “er sterben wollte” — wollen here is not ‘wanted to’ in the modern sense but the older ‘was about to, was going to.’ “bei mir bedacht” is to have thought a thing over within oneself; “eröffnen” in this older sense is to disclose, to make known.

sentences.t: welcher von euch der Faulste ist, der soll nach mir König werden.“
sentences.l: whichever of you is the laziest, he shall become king after me.”
sentences.i: whichever of you is the laziest shall be king after me.”
sentences.n: German picks the clause up again with “der” — ‘whoever of you …, that one shall …’ — a doubling English simply drops. “nach mir” is ‘after me’ in time, that is, as my successor.

sentences.t: Da sprach der älteste „Vater, so gehört das Reich mir, denn ich bin so faul,
sentences.l: Then the eldest said “father, then the kingdom belongs to me, for I am so lazy,
sentences.i: Then the eldest said, “Father, in that case the realm is mine, for I am so lazy:
sentences.n: “so gehört das Reich mir” — “so” draws the consequence, ‘in that case.’ “gehört” is gehören, to belong, taking the dative “mir”; it is not the past participle of hören.

sentences.t: wenn ich liege und will schlafen, und es fällt mir ein Tropfen in die Augen, so mag ich sie nicht zuthun, damit ich einschlafe.“
sentences.l: when I lie down and want to sleep, and a drop falls into my eyes, then I do not care to shut them, so that I might fall asleep.”
sentences.i: when I am lying down and want to sleep, and a drop falls into my eyes, I cannot be troubled to close them so as to fall asleep.”
sentences.n: “fällt mir ein Tropfen in die Augen” is a dative of possession again — a drop falls into the eyes ‘to me.’ “mag ich nicht” is not ‘may not’ but ‘have no inclination to.’ “zuthun” is the 1857 spelling of zutun, to shut. The absurdity is that closing his eyes is what would let him sleep.

sentences.t: Der zweite sprach „Vater, das Reich gehört mir, denn ich bin so faul,
sentences.l: The second said “father, the kingdom belongs to me, for I am so lazy,
sentences.i: The second said, “Father, the realm is mine, for I am so lazy:
sentences.n: Each brother opens with the same claim in slightly different words; the tale runs the pattern three times and lets the boasts escalate.

sentences.t: wenn ich beim Feuer sitze mich zu wärmen, so ließ ich mir eher die Fersen verbrennen, eh ich die Beine zurück zöge.“
sentences.l: when I sit by the fire to warm myself, then I would sooner let my heels burn than that I would draw my legs back.”
sentences.i: when I sit by the fire to warm myself, I would sooner let my heels burn than draw my legs back.”
sentences.n: “ließ” and “zöge” are subjunctives — would let, would draw — in the older forms without würde. “eher … eh” is ‘sooner … than’; “eh” is the short form of ehe. “zurück zöge” is zurückziehen pulled apart.

sentences.t: Der dritte sprach „Vater, das Reich ist mein, denn ich bin so faul,
sentences.l: The third said “father, the kingdom is mine, for I am so lazy,
sentences.i: The third said, “Father, the realm is mine, for I am so lazy:
sentences.n: The third drops the verb of belonging altogether — “das Reich ist mein,” simply ‘the realm is mine.’

sentences.t: sollt ich aufgehenkt werden, und hätte den Strick schon um den Hals, und einer gäbe mir ein scharf Messer in die Hand, damit ich den Strick zerschneiden dürfte,
sentences.l: were I to be hanged, and had the rope already round my neck, and someone gave me a sharp knife into my hand, so that I might cut the rope through,
sentences.i: if I were to be hanged, and had the rope round my neck already, and someone put a sharp knife into my hand so that I might cut the rope,
sentences.n: A conditional built without wenn: the verb comes first (“sollt ich …”), and English marks it with ‘if’ or by inverting. “ein scharf Messer” leaves the adjective uninflected, an older usage where modern German has “ein scharfes Messer.”

sentences.t: so ließ ich mich eher aufhenken, eh ich meine Hand erhübe zum Strick.“
sentences.l: then I would sooner let myself be hanged than that I would raise my hand to the rope.”
sentences.i: I would sooner let myself be hanged than lift my hand to the rope.”
sentences.n: “erhübe” is the old subjunctive of erheben, would raise; modern German would say erhöbe or würde erheben. Two different verbs for hanging stand two lines apart, “aufgehenkt” and “aufhenken,” both older beside modern aufhängen.

sentences.t: Wie der Vater das hörte sprach er „du hast es am weitesten gebracht und sollst der König sein.“
sentences.l: When the father heard that he said “you have brought it the furthest and shall be the king.”
sentences.i: When the father heard that, he said, “You have carried it furthest, and you shall be king.”
sentences.n: “es weit bringen” is a set phrase — to get far, to go a long way in the world — and “am weitesten” is its superlative. The father pays the third son the compliment usually paid to the industrious, which is the joke the tale ends on.

glossary.bedacht: bedenken — considered, thought over (past part.; „bei sich bedacht“ = turned over in one’s mind)
glossary.es: es — it (also the impersonal subject, as in „es fällt ein Tropfen“ = a drop falls)
glossary.gebracht: bringen — brought (past part.); „es weit bringen“ = to get far, go a long way
glossary.gehört: gehören — belongs (3rd sg. pres., + dative); not the past participle of hören
glossary.mag: mögen — care to, have a mind to (1st/3rd sg. pres.; „mag ich nicht“ = I do not care to)
glossary.welchen: welcher — which one (masc. acc. sg. welchen; „welchen er bestimmen sollte“ = which one he should appoint)
glossary.welcher: welcher — whichever, which (masc. nom. sg.; „welcher von euch“ = whichever of you)
glossary.zöge: ziehen — would draw, pull (past subjunctive); zurückziehen = to draw back
